points.title: Memory address and memory location
points.must: Location stores fixed bits (usually 1 byte); address = unique number identifying a location; address ≠ contents; random access.
points.model: Memory location = unit of main memory storing a fixed number of bits (usually 1 byte). Memory address = unique number that identifies one location. The address is where, the contents is what is stored (location 30 holds 45). Any address reached directly → random-access memory.

points.title: Address bus, data bus, control bus
points.must: Address bus carries address CPU → memory (one way); data bus carries contents both ways; control bus carries read/write and clock.
points.model: Address bus: carries the address from CPU to memory, one-way. Data bus: carries data/instructions between CPU and memory, two-way. Control bus: carries control signals — memory read, memory write, clock.

points.title: MAR and MDR
points.must: MAR holds the address of the location to be used; MDR holds data just read or to be written.
points.model: MAR (Memory Address Register) = holds the address of the location to be read/written (placed on the address bus). MDR (Memory Data Register) = holds the data read from or to be written to memory (connected to the data bus).

points.title: Steps of a memory read and write
points.must: Read: address → MAR → address bus, read signal, contents → data bus → MDR. Write: address → MAR, data → MDR, write signal, old contents overwritten.
points.model: Read: address copied to MAR → address bus → memory read signal on control bus → contents placed on data bus → MDR. Write: address to MAR, data to MDR → memory write signal → data stored, old contents overwritten.

points.title: Byte-addressable vs word-addressable; word
points.must: Word = bits CPU handles as one unit; byte-addressable: each byte has an address (8-byte word uses 8 addresses); word-addressable: each address holds a word.
points.model: Word = number of bits the CPU processes as one unit (16/32/64). Byte-addressable: every byte has its own address — a 64-bit word occupies 8 addresses (1000–1007); most modern computers. Word-addressable: each address holds one whole word.

points.title: Address bus width and maximum memory
points.must: n lines → 2ⁿ addresses; max memory = 2ⁿ × location size; +1 line doubles; table 16 → 64 KiB, 20 → 1 MiB, 32 → 4 GiB; worked examples (24-bit × 2 bytes = 32 MiB; 256 MiB → 28 lines).
points.model: n address lines → 2ⁿ addresses. Max memory = 2ⁿ × size of each location. One more line doubles the addresses. 16 bits → 64 KiB; 20 → 1 MiB; 24 → 16 MiB; 32 → 4 GiB. 24-bit bus, 2-byte words: 2²⁴ × 2 = 32 MiB. 256 MiB = 2²⁸ → 28 lines.

points.title: Opcode, operand and addressing mode
points.must: Opcode = what to do; operand = data or address; addressing mode = how the CPU interprets the operand to find the data.
points.model: Opcode = the operation (load, add, jump). Operand = the number the instruction works on. Addressing mode = the method the CPU uses to interpret the operand to find the data (value, address, address of address, + index).

points.title: Immediate, direct and indirect addressing
points.must: Immediate: operand is the value (LDM #30, fastest, constants); direct: operand is the address (LDD 30, variables); indirect: operand is address of the address (LDI 30, pointers, two accesses).
points.model: Immediate: operand IS the value — LDM #30 → ACC = 30; no memory access; constants. Direct: operand is the address of the value — LDD 30 → contents of 30; simple variables. Indirect: operand is the address of a location holding the address — LDI 30 → contents of (contents of 30); pointers, large addresses; 2 memory accesses.

points.title: Indexed and relative addressing
points.must: Indexed: address = operand + IX (arrays, loops); relative: address = PC + offset (jumps, relocatable code).
points.model: Indexed: address = operand + index register (IX) — LDX 30 with IX = 3 → contents of 33; increment IX to step through an array. Relative: address = address of current instruction (PC) + offset — JMR 5; jumps in loops; relocatable code.

points.title: Stored-program concept (von Neumann)
points.must: Instructions and data in the same memory in binary; fetched one at a time, decoded, executed; same buses; principles: CPU tells instruction from data by PC/fetch, sequential execution, program changed by loading new one.
points.model: Stored-program concept: program instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory in binary; the CPU fetches instructions one at a time, decodes and executes them, using the same buses. A word is an instruction when the PC points to it in the fetch stage. Executed in sequence (PC incremented) unless a jump. New program = load into memory, no rewiring.

points.title: Fetch–decode–execute and program areas
points.must: PC → MAR → instruction into MDR → CIR, PC incremented, decode, execute; program in memory: code, data, stack, heap areas.
points.model: FDE: PC → MAR; instruction read into MDR → CIR; PC incremented; control unit decodes; execute (data read/written if needed); repeat. Memory areas of a program: code (can be read-only), data, stack, heap.

points.title: Von Neumann bottleneck and Harvard architecture
points.must: Bottleneck = shared memory and bus → instruction and data cannot be fetched together, CPU waits; reduced by cache/pipelining. Harvard = separate memories and buses → simultaneous fetch, faster, but complex/fixed split; used in microcontrollers, DSPs, L1 cache.
points.model: Von Neumann bottleneck: instructions and data share one memory and bus → cannot be fetched at the same time → CPU waits (reduced by cache, pipelining). Harvard: separate instruction and data memories and buses → fetched at the same time → faster; more complex, fixed memory split. Used in microcontrollers, DSPs, embedded systems, split L1 cache.
